column1: Is Agile a software development methodology?
column2: No. It is an approach or characteristic you apply to a development process to make it agile or not.

column1: What does the word "agile" literally mean, per the lecturer?
column2: Anything that is quick and nimble.

column1: How should you reinterpret the question "do you follow an agile methodology?"
column2: As "is your software development process following agile thinking?"

column1: What is a "process" in the general sense?
column2: A sequence of steps for doing something — not a software-specific term.

column1: Name two traditional software process models mentioned in the lecture.
column2: Waterfall and spiral.

column1: How is agile thinking communicated to industry?
column2: Through the agile values and principles.

column1: What is the dependency between agile values and principles?
column2: Values guide the generation (definition) of the principles.

column1: Where was the Agile Manifesto published?
column2: agilemanifesto.org, around 2002–2003; the site is essentially unchanged since.

column1: How many agile values are there?
column2: Four.

column1: State agile value 1.
column2: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.

column1: State agile value 2.
column2: Working software over comprehensive documentation.

column1: State agile value 3.
column2: Customer collaboration over contract negotiation.

column1: State agile value 4.
column2: Responding to change over following a plan.

column1: What does "over" mean in the agile values?
column2: Both sides are valuable; the value states which one wins when they collide — not that the right side is worthless.

column1: Under agile value 1, what is the team's leadership structure?
column2: No one is leading the team and no one is left behind; everyone has an equal say.

column1: What analogy justifies preferring individuals over tools?
column2: Limited resources plus high motivation beats abundant resources plus low motivation.

column1: Which specific document does agile value 2 target?
column2: The Software Requirements Specification (SRS), when it absorbs early effort that should go into implementation.

column1: Define "working software" as used in this lecture.
column2: A build that compiles successfully, runs successfully, and is available to the other team members.

column1: In this course, who represents the client, and what roles do they play?
column2: The Product Owner — playing customer, client and user simultaneously.

column1: Why are course Product Owners kept out of the sprint itself?
column2: They are mostly non-technical, so being inside the sprint serves no purpose; they belong in sprint reviews.

column1: What is the failure mode of "contract negotiation"?
column2: A rigid contract that forbids any later changes to the requirements.

column1: How many agile principles are there?
column2: Twelve.

column1: What is the agile "highest priority" principle?
column2: Satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.

column1: What sprint length does the Agile Manifesto suggest?
column2: A couple of weeks to a couple of months.

column1: What is the typical industry sprint length mentioned?
column2: Around four weeks, depending on project scale.

column1: What sprint length does SOFTENG 761 use?
column2: One week — below the manifesto's own lower bound.

column1: What is the primary measure of progress in agile?
column2: Working software.

column1: What does principle 6 require, and what qualification did the lecturer add?
column2: Face-to-face conversation; it may be online rather than physically co-located.

column1: Are the agile principles part of the contract with the client?
column2: No — they guide the process; the actual limits come from your interaction with the product owner.

column1: What agile concept does small, frequent committing implement?
column2: Continuous integration.

column1: How large should a commit be?
column2: The smallest possible chunk, with the build unbroken and tests passing.

column1: Give the two benefits of committing small and often.
column2: Nobody is ever blocked cloning the repo, and the team is always ready to demo the latest version.

column1: What is the commit anti-pattern seen in student teams?
column2: Working locally for days or weeks and then pushing one large commit.

column1: Name the two costs of the single-large-commit anti-pattern.
column2: It often breaks the build, and it leaves almost no evidence of regular work.

column1: What is the best evidence of your contribution to a project?
column2: Your commits.

column1: Why is a "planning only, no coding" role dangerous at marking time?
column2: It leaves no commits, so your contribution is not visible and you lose marks.

column1: Which methodology supplies pair programming and code reviews?
column2: Extreme Programming (XP).

column1: When should a team agree its code-quality standards?
column2: In the first team meeting — code quality is a marked component.

column1: Can a Scrum team assign code review to specific members?
column2: Yes — although everyone is responsible for everything, the team may agree that 1–2 members review regularly.

column1: What is the prescribed response to an unavailable Product Owner?
column2: Be ahead of the game: in meeting one, establish their availability and the rule for proceeding without them.

column1: What must exist before you can agree "can we go ahead without you?"
column2: At least a draft product backlog from the first meeting.

column1: Give the two brakes on scope creep.
column2: An explicit up-front agreement that changes happen "wherever possible", and the PO's own interest in completion since they will own the product.

column1: Which kind of late change may you legitimately push back on?
column2: A technology switch — be sceptical, but say changes can be made wherever possible.

column1: In which meeting do change and scope conversations happen?
column2: The sprint review.

column1: What is a user story?
column2: Another name for an individual requirement, written in a developer-friendly one-line form.

column1: Give the three slots of a user story.
column2: Who (the user/role), what (the functionality), why (why it matters).

column1: Write the standard user story sentence frame.
column2: As a <user>, I want <functionality>, so that <reason>.

column1: Why does the "who" slot matter?
column2: Different user types need different interfaces and functionality; encoding the role keeps them distinct.

column1: What is the relationship between requirements and user stories?
column2: Each requirement can be split into multiple user stories.

column1: What do you do with user stories before moving them to a sprint backlog?
column2: Prioritise them, with input from the product owner.

column1: What is an acceptance criterion for?
column2: Deciding whether an implementation actually validates its user story.

column1: What is the primary advantage of writing acceptance criteria early?
column2: They translate very easily into unit tests or integration tests.

column1: What turns a user story into an acceptance criterion?
column2: Specificity — a named actor, the actual content, the actual stakeholders.

column1: What does test-driven development start from?
column2: The acceptance criteria, written before going into the details of the functionality.

column1: What does the Code Runner example illustrate?
column2: When tests are visible and finite, people pass exactly those tests and ignore edge and boundary cases.

column1: Are acceptance criteria a floor or a ceiling?
column2: A floor — the minimum a correct implementation must satisfy.

column1: Who decides how much testing is enough?
column2: The product owner.

column1: Define Scrum as the lecturer does.
column2: A lightweight framework defined around people and their communication.

column1: Which agile value is Scrum built most directly on?
column2: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.

column1: What is a Scrum Master?
column2: A facilitator who removes impediments and runs the events — explicitly not the leader of the team.

column1: State the Scrum leadership formula.
column2: Everyone is a leader and there is no leader.

column1: Who is responsible for maximising the value of the product resulting from the dev team's work?
column2: The Product Owner.

column1: What does "self-organising" mean in Scrum?
column2: The team organises its own roles by communication at the start of the cycle; roles are not dictated to them.

column1: During sprint planning, who selects how much work is taken on?
column2: The development team — not the PO, and not by per-developer task assignment.

column1: Name two agile processes other than Scrum mentioned in the lecture.
column2: Kanban and Scrumban.

column1: Why do industry teams often keep an old process?
column2: Inertia — a team is used to a specific process and changing is very difficult.

column1: Which Canvas resource is the standing textual reference for Scrum?
column2: The Scrum Primer, under Module 3.

column1: Name the three pillars of Scrum.
column2: Transparency, inspection, adaptation.

column1: What does transparency require concretely?
column2: Every member's progress visible to everyone else, via a tool such as a board plus a definition of done.

column1: What is an "opaque sub-team" and why is it a problem?
column2: A sub-group inside a large team that is transparent to itself but opaque to the rest — it breaks global transparency.

column1: What does the inspection pillar amount to in practice?
column2: Regularly reviewing each other's work; code reviews.

column1: Which pillar does the lecturer call tricky, and why?
column2: Adaptation — teams must absorb technology switches, role changes and new PO requirements mid-flight.

column1: Name the three types of software maintenance.
column2: Corrective, adaptive, perfective.

column1: What triggers corrective maintenance?
column2: Something is wrong — flagged by the PO at a review, or found in your own retrospective or daily scrum.

column1: What triggers adaptive maintenance?
column2: A change in environment, technology or team members.

column1: What triggers perfective maintenance?
column2: Nothing — a developer improves something unprompted because they have time and motivation.

column1: Why is perfective maintenance a hazard in a Scrum team?
column2: It was never discussed or agreed, so it surprises the team; the objection is to the invisibility, not the improvement.

column1: When is perfective maintenance acceptable?
column2: When the PO has asked for creativity and the rest of the team knows you are doing it.

column1: Distinguish "adaptation" from "adaptive maintenance".
column2: Adaptation is a property of the process (a Scrum pillar); adaptive maintenance is a category of code change.

column1: What is the purpose of sprint planning?
column2: Define what will be delivered in the sprint and how it will be achieved.

column1: How long is the daily scrum, and when is it held?
column2: 15 minutes, at the start of each day.

column1: Who attends the daily scrum?
column2: The development team only — the PO is deliberately not invited.

column1: What happens in a sprint review?
column2: The team demonstrates the increment to the PO and stakeholders, who inspect it and adapt the backlog if needed.

column1: What does the sprint retrospective inspect?
column2: The team itself — it is a timeboxed opportunity to inspect itself and plan improvements.

column1: Distinguish sprint review from sprint retrospective in one line.
column2: Review inspects the product; retrospective inspects the team.

column1: Define the product backlog.
column2: An ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product.

column1: Define the sprint backlog.
column2: The user stories pulled into one specific sprint.

column1: Define an increment.
column2: The working software produced at the end of a sprint.

column1: Who crafts the Definition of Done?
column2: The whole development team — every member shares the responsibility.

column1: Which artefact gives a transparent view of the current state of the product?
column2: The increment.

column1: Why isn't the velocity chart the answer to "current state of the product"?
column2: It only shows how many points were completed — throughput, not product state.

column1: When do weekly increment presentations start in this course?
column2: From week 6, after reviewing with the product owner.

column1: What does a sprint burn-down chart show?
column2: How much backlog work remains and at what rate it is being reduced.

column1: A burn-down shows work remaining increasing over several days. What should the Scrum Master do?
column2: Address impediments and facilitate a team discussion on blockers.

column1: Why shouldn't the Scrum Master extend the sprint when work is overrunning?
column2: It impacts the later sprints and the overall project timeline.

column1: Why shouldn't the Scrum Master reassign work to "faster developers"?
column2: Faster is undefinable, it may create new problems, and it demoralises the team member.

column1: What is the cleanest one-line definition of the Scrum Master's job from this lecture?
column2: They do not know what the discussion will produce, but their job is to facilitate it.

column1: What likelihood does the lecturer give to a team member falling ill during the semester?
What is the structural mitigation for member unavailability in an 8-person team?
column2: Work in pairs so every member has at least one backup.

column1: When must an unresolvable team problem be escalated to course staff?
column2: Early — by week ten it is too late for them to help.

column1: Which meeting is the right place to fix process problems?
column2: The sprint retrospective.

column1: Which Scrum event does NOT include the product owner?
column2: The daily scrum.
